query: In high-entropy alloys, what governs superconducting behavior and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, identify a controlled comparison against a baseline that could reveal the governing cause, predict the relative observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, define its boundary conditions, state what prior evidence would make it plausible, and specify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing short-range chemical ordering in high-entropy alloys reduces local structural disorder and enhances electron–phonon coupling, thereby raising the superconducting transition temperature (Tc) relative to more disordered states.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase high-entropy alloy sample in the as-cast (minimally ordered) condition, exhibiting conventional electron–phonon coupling-based superconductivity.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary short-range order by applying controlled annealing at different temperatures and durations, followed by quenching, and subsequently measure local atomic arrangement via synchrotron X-ray and neutron total scattering while determining Tc via low-temperature electronic transport measurements or magnetic susceptibility.
generation.conditions: All samples measured in the 2–10 K temperature range under identical cryogenic and magnetic field conditions to isolate changes in Tc attributable to short-range ordering.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical clustering and short-range ordering within the lattice.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced short-range ordering reduces atomic-scale disorder and optimizes the local bonding environment, improving electron–phonon coupling and increasing the energy gap associated with the superconducting state.
generation.predicted_outcome: Annealed samples with greater short-range order will display a systematically higher Tc than the as-cast (more disordered) baseline. The magnitude of the shift in Tc should correlate with the degree of local structural ordering revealed by total scattering data.
generation.baseline: As-cast, unannealed high-entropy alloy sample exhibiting low short-range order and lower Tc.
generation.boundary: The effect is most discernible in multi-principal-element alloys dominated by electron–phonon coupling. If additional complexities (magnetic order, strong electron correlations, or pronounced spin–orbit coupling) become dominant, the relationship between short-range ordering and superconductivity may weaken or invert.
generation.uncertainty: Other compositional factors, such as specific elemental substitutions or f-electron contributions, may offset or complicate the impact of short-range ordering and require further study for conclusive determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical alloy batches, subject each to increasing annealing temperatures to systematically alter short-range ordering, measure local structure with total scattering, and measure Tc in each specimen.
measurements: Pair distribution function (PDF) or neutron total scattering for local structural ordering
Temperature-dependent electrical resistivity or magnetic susceptibility for Tc
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples with higher levels of short-range order do not exhibit any systematic increase in Tc compared to disordered reference samples or if changes in local ordering are not correlated with changes in Tc, the hypothesis is falsified.

The superconductivity of disordered materials has been extensively studied because of an observation made on the insulator-superconductor transition or disorder-induced superconductivity. In addition, recent studies on BiS2-based layered superconductors have shown the importance of controlling the local structural disorder to improve superconducting properties. As a new category of disordered superconductors, high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which are alloys containing five or more elements with an atomic concentration between 5 and 35%,, have been extensively studied, leading to the discovery of a wide range of HEA superconductors. One of the notable features is the difference in characteristics of superconductivity among conventional metal or alloy superconductors, superconducting thin films, and HEA superconductors,. Namely, the dependence of Tc on valence electron count (VEC) for HEAs exhibits interesting trends when that was compared with those for classical alloys (metals) and amorphous alloys. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are a new type of alloy with five or more chemical elements arranged on a pseudocrystalline lattice. A high mixing-entropy minimizes the Gibbs free-energy and facilitates their crystallization on simple lattice structures, such as body-centered cubic (bcc) structure,,,. Despite the significant amount of compositional disorder, a subset of the HEAs enters a type-II superconducting phase at cryogenic temperatures,. Their large critical fields combined with superior mechanical and thermal properties render HEA promising candidates for materials applications under extreme conditions, for the fabrication of superconducting magnets, and for superconducting devices based on HEA thin films. Ongoing materials synthesis efforts have extended the family of known superconducting HEAs and developed a phenomenological understanding of their properties,. Various analyses of the upper critical field Hc2 and heat capacity measurements as a function of temperature T support a conventional Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer (BCS) pairing mechanism,,, with intermediate-strong coupling. decision.trend: Only one of the earlier papers (PMC7070041) directly addresses superconductivity in high-entropy alloys, reporting phonon-mediated, BCS-like superconductivity in a uranium-containing high-entropy alloy with notable involvement of strong spin-orbit coupling. This result showed that mixing multiple principal elements—potentially including f-electron species—can sustain robust superconductivity. However, it also left open questions on how local chemical environments, atomic disorder, spin-orbit effects, and electron-phonon coupling collectively govern superconducting properties in high-entropy alloys.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear whether the primary driver for the superconducting transition temperature is local structural disorder, chemical short-range ordering, spin-orbit coupling, or some interplay among these factors in multi-principal-element alloys, particularly when f-electron elements are introduced.
decision.lever: Perform synchrotron/X-ray pair distribution function (PDF) and neutron total scattering measurements on the same high-entropy alloy samples under different annealing histories (to vary short-range order) while measuring superconducting transition temperatures in situ or ex situ.
decision.why: Such an approach directly probes local atomic arrangements in tandem with superconducting properties, which can clarify the connection between local bonding/chemical order and electron-phonon coupling. Varying short-range order via heat treatments provides a controlled way to test the hypothesis that local disorder modulates the superconducting state. If Tₐ adaptation (and associated changes in short-range ordering) systematically shifts Tc in line with changes in local order, that outcome would confirm disorder-driven superconductivity. If no measurable shift in Tc occurs despite significant structural changes, it would argue that the controlling factor is dominated by other mechanisms.
